title: Reading from the South: How Africa, Asia and Latin America Read the Bible
standfirst: Culture and the Bible in the Global South
subtitle: The shift of the church's centre southward, Walls's indigenizing and pilgrim principles, Sanneh on translation, African, Asian and Latin American readings from Bediako and Koyama to Gutiérrez and integral mission, Jenkins on a world closer to the text, and what North and South can learn from and warn each other about.

sections.title: The Centre Moves, and the Reading With It
sections.body:
When the World Missionary Conference met at Edinburgh in 1910, most delegates took it for granted that the West would remain the faith's heartland and its teacher, sending out a Bible the rest of the world would learn to read more or less as the West read it. Within a lifetime the assumption had been overturned. By the later decades of the century, on the standard estimates of historians such as Andrew Walls and Philip Jenkins, most of the world's Christians lived in Africa, Asia and Latin America, and the Bible was being read in languages, villages and crises the Edinburgh delegates never pictured.

Walls, a Scottish historian who had taught in Sierra Leone and Nigeria before founding a centre for the study of Christianity beyond the West, first at Aberdeen and then at Edinburgh, gave the church a vocabulary for what happened next. In an essay collected in The Missionary Movement in Christian History, he described two forces at work in every Christian community. The indigenizing principle is the gospel's determination to be at home in every culture, because God accepts people as they are, with their language, kin and history. The pilgrim principle is the gospel's equal determination to make every believer a little homeless in his own culture, because the God who accepts us as we are does not leave us there. Both come from the same gospel. Neither can be surrendered without loss.

Those two principles are the key to this essay. They mean that every reading of Scripture is a cultural reading, including the West's, and that no culture's reading is final, including anyone else's. The Western reader tends to notice the culture in an African or Korean interpretation while assuming his own interpretation is simply what the text says. A century of Southern Christianity has made that assumption much harder to keep.

sections.title: A Faith Without a Sacred Language
sections.body:
Lamin Sanneh came to the question from an unusual place. Born in the Gambia and raised a Muslim, he became a Christian and spent his career as a historian, eventually at Yale. In Translating the Message, published in 1989, he argued that Christianity is distinctive among the great religions in having no sacred language. The words of Jesus, spoken in Aramaic, reached the church in Greek. At Pentecost, in Acts 2, the crowd heard the apostles each in his own tongue. From the beginning the faith assumed that the word of God could be carried whole into any human language, and Sanneh set this beside the Islam of his upbringing, in which the Qur'an is recited in worship in Arabic wherever Muslims live.

The consequences, in Sanneh's account, were larger than the missionaries knew. To translate the Bible into Yoruba, Kikuyu or Korean, missionaries had to learn the language from its speakers, produce grammars and dictionaries, and find in the local vocabulary a name for God. In doing so they conceded that the receiving language was worthy of Scripture. Translation dignified the vernacular and, without intending to, placed in local hands the instrument by which local readers could judge the missionaries themselves.

Sanneh did not deny that missions were often entangled with colonial power, and the critics who press that point are describing something real. His argument was that the colonial story is not the whole story, and that the act of translation kept working against the paternalism of the translators. A Bible in a people's own tongue belonged to them. What they would find in it, no mission board could control.

sections.title: The Bible in African Hands
sections.body:
African theologians of the late twentieth century set themselves a double task: to read the Bible as Africans and to show that doing so was faithful to it. John Mbiti, the Kenyan scholar whose African Religions and Philosophy appeared in 1969, argued that Africa's traditional religions had known God long before missionaries arrived, and that the gospel therefore entered a world already prepared to hear of the Creator. Kwame Bediako of Ghana pressed the case further in Christianity in Africa, published in 1995 with the subtitle The Renewal of a Non-Western Religion. Bediako argued that Africa's primal religions formed a kind of substructure for African Christianity, much as Greek philosophy had for the early fathers, and that African theologians were working through questions of identity the second-century church had faced. He read the Letter to the Hebrews, with its one great high priest who has passed through death, as speaking directly to a world that honored its ancestors: Christ does not erase the question of the ancestors, he answers it.

The African Independent Churches, founded by Africans outside the mission denominations, read with a different closeness. In the Aladura churches of Nigeria, the Zionist churches of southern Africa and the Kimbanguist church of the Congo, the world of the Old Testament seemed familiar rather than remote. Prophets, dreams, healing, purity rules, the obligations of clan and household, the anointing of leaders: these were not exotic to them.

That closeness is a gift, and the African church has also had to weigh it. Some independent movements moved toward syncretism, and African theologians have been among their most careful critics. The pilgrim principle applies in Lagos as it does in London.

sections.title: Water Buffalo and the Dawn Prayer
sections.body:
Kosuke Koyama, a Japanese theologian, went to northern Thailand as a missionary teacher in 1960. There he decided that he had to begin with the rice farmers in front of him, and with the water buffalo standing in their fields, rather than with the great theologians he had studied in the West. Water Buffalo Theology, published in 1974, is the record of that decision. Koyama tried to speak of Christ in the categories of a Buddhist agricultural world, its cycles of rain and harvest and its longing for detachment, and he insisted that the theologian's first question was whether he loved his neighbor enough to learn how that neighbor thought. Later he would describe the God of Israel as a God who walks at three miles an hour, the speed at which love travels.

Korea offers a different chapter. In January 1907, at a Bible study conference in Pyongyang, a revival broke out marked by long public confession of sin, and it spread through the young Korean church. The movement grew out of practices that would define Korean Protestantism: intensive Bible classes for ordinary believers, daily prayer before dawn, and a Bible printed in hangul, the Korean alphabet that the educated elite had long ranked below Chinese characters. Sanneh's argument about the vernacular could have no clearer illustration.

Under Japanese rule, from 1910 to 1945, Korean believers read the Exodus and the prophets as words for a captive people, and in the 1930s many refused to bow at the Shinto shrines the empire required. The pastor Ju Gi-cheol was imprisoned for that refusal and died in prison in 1944. The first commandment was, for them, a matter of life and death.

sections.title: Reading From the Underside of History
sections.body:
In 1971 the Peruvian priest Gustavo Gutiérrez published A Theology of Liberation, and it became one of the most influential theological books to come out of Latin America. The case deserves to be stated as its defenders would state it. Gutiérrez served in Lima, on a continent of deep poverty and inequality, where the church had often stood beside the landowners and the generals. He argued that theology is critical reflection on Christian practice in the light of the word of God, and that the Bible itself discloses a God who hears the cry of the oppressed. The Exodus is the founding event of Israel's faith. Jesus opens his ministry in Luke 4 by announcing good news to the poor and liberty to the captives. To read this Bible as if poverty were merely a spiritual metaphor, Gutiérrez contended, was itself a reading shaped by the comfortable. At Medellín in 1968 the Latin American bishops had moved the same way, and base communities of poor Catholics began reading Scripture together with their own lives as the commentary.

The serious criticism deserves the same fairness. In 1984 the Vatican's Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, under Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger, warned against borrowing Marxist analysis uncritically, against making class struggle the key to the text, and against reducing salvation to political deliverance. A second instruction in 1986 was more appreciative of the movement's concern for the poor.

The weighing cuts in more than one direction. The danger of reading the Exodus through an ideology is real. It is the same danger, from the other side, that an antebellum South or a Cold War West ran when it read Scripture as a defense of its own order. Gutiérrez himself grew more insistent that the option for the poor rests on the free love of God, and his 1986 book on Job is a meditation on grace as much as on justice.

sections.title: Integral Mission
sections.body:
Evangelical Latin Americans were reading the same continent and the same Bible, and they arrived somewhere distinct. In 1970 a group of them founded the Latin American Theological Fraternity in Bolivia, and two of its leading voices, René Padilla of Ecuador and Samuel Escobar of Peru, carried its convictions to the International Congress on World Evangelization at Lausanne in July 1974.

What they said there unsettled many of their hosts. Padilla warned against a culture Christianity that confused the gospel with the American way of life and spread both together. Escobar pressed the point that evangelism could not be cut away from the call to justice without mutilating the gospel Jesus preached. Both were evangelicals in the full sense, committed to the authority of Scripture and the necessity of personal conversion, and both refused the choice their Western brethren had inherited from the fundamentalist and modernist quarrels between saving souls and serving bodies. The name that came to describe their position was misión integral, integral mission: the whole gospel, for the whole person, in the whole of life, with the kingdom of God as the centre that holds them together.

The Lausanne Covenant, drafted chiefly by John Stott, bore their mark. Its fifth paragraph affirmed that evangelism and sociopolitical involvement are both part of Christian duty, and it expressed penitence for having sometimes regarded them as mutually exclusive.

Integral mission was a third reading, neither the Western evangelical individualism that treated the poverty texts as illustrations nor the liberationist method that took its analysis of society from Marx. It read Luke 4 as both evangelical and economic. And it came, notably, from the South to the North, a correction offered by the younger churches to the older ones in the older ones' own idiom.

sections.title: A World Closer to the Text
sections.body:
In The New Faces of Christianity, published in 2006, Philip Jenkins asked a simple question with large consequences: what happens when the Bible is read by people whose daily lives resemble the world it describes? His answer was that many Southern readers find that world nearer to their own than Western readers do. They know famine, and so the Book of Ruth, which opens with a family driven abroad by hunger, reads to them as a migrant's story. They know corrupt rulers, the threat of persecution, the weight of debt, and the reality of spiritual powers, and so the Gospels' exorcisms, the Psalms of protection and the Letter of James on rich and poor land with an immediacy a comfortable reader can miss.

Jenkins also noticed that Southern readers frustrate Western categories. Many are conservative on questions of sexuality and the family, and many are radical on questions of wealth and power. They read the Bible's moral law and its economic justice as one book, and Westerners of both left and right find half of them uncomfortable. The 1998 Lambeth Conference, where African and Asian Anglican bishops were prominent in the large majority that passed a traditional resolution on sexuality, made that visible to the whole Anglican world.

Set beside this the claim Rudolf Bultmann made in his 1941 essay on the New Testament and mythology, that modern people who use electric light and the radio cannot also believe in the New Testament's world of spirits and miracles. Much of the Southern church uses electric light and believes it. Bultmann thought he was describing the modern mind. Read from Lagos or Seoul, he was describing a province of it.

sections.title: What Each Can Learn
sections.body:
The West has a great deal to learn here, and the first lesson is humility about its own location. Charles Taylor has described the modern Western self as buffered, sealed off from spirits and powers, and much Western reading of Scripture quietly skips the texts that offend that self: the demons, the healings, the warnings to the rich. A Western pastor like me reads the Bible through the categories of a prosperous, individualist, therapeutic culture, and I am usually the last to notice. My Southern brothers and sisters notice at once.

But the same instrument has to be turned on the South, or it is flattery. The prosperity gospel, the teaching that faith secures health and wealth, has spread widely through the Southern churches, from West Africa to Brazil to Korea. It is a serious error, and this platform names it as one. Its pedigree is partly ours. Much of it was carried south by American preachers, and it found soil where poverty met older expectations that spiritual power should yield material blessing. In Walls's terms it is indigenization without pilgrimage, the gospel made so much at home that it no longer calls anyone out. Some of its sharpest critics are African and Latin American pastors.

The Western therapeutic gospel and the Western nationalist gospel are the same failure in a different accent. Every culture that reads the Bible is tempted to hear its own desires as God's voice. No culture is exempt, and none is disqualified.

The church that reads well will read together, across the regions and the centuries, each culture exposing what the others cannot see. It means letting a farmer in Thailand or a grandmother in Ghana correct my sermon. The great multitude of Revelation 7, from every nation and tribe and language, will stand before one throne. We are not yet ready to stand there together.
